newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK interest rates rise for fourth month.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK interest rates rise for fourth month.

text.p: The Bank of England raised official interest rates on Thursday for the fourth month in a row but delivered a strong hint that this would be the last policy tightening for some time.
The Bank's new Monetary Policy Committee, which was empowered by the Labour government in May to determine monetary policy, raised official interest rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent.
The committee acknowledged that the strong pound was putting severe pressure on exporters but said this was largely due to factors outside the influence of British policy-makers.

"In the light of the prospect for domestic demand and on the basis of all the evidence currently available, the committee judges that today's rise is necessary to put the economy on track for achieving the inflation target of 2.5 percent looking two years ahead," it said.

In a clear signal to financial markets that it had no immediate plans for further rate rises, the committee said: "Upward pressures on the exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target."
Financial markets appeared to get the message.

The pound, which has surged around 25 percent against major currencies in the past year, slipped nearly two pfennigs against the deutschemark to around 2.99 marks compared with 3.01 just before the announcement.
London share prices also surged, with the FTSE 100 index setting a fresh record of 5.049.5, a rise of 23.3 points from beforehand.

"This is a clear signal that the Bank thinks it has done enough for the time being and it believes the move should put downward pressure on sterling," said Ciaran Barr, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "We do not expect another rate rise until November."

Bank of England Governor Eddie George, who chairs the monetary policy committee, has expressed concern that rampant consumer spending will fuel a resurgence in inflation, which is at historically low levels in Britain at the moment.

But some economists argue that consumer spending growth is fuelled by one-off "windfall" gains totalling an estimated 35 billion pounds ($56 billion), which millions of Britons are receiving this year as mutually owned building societies turn themselves into banks. They believe the impact of the windfalls will largely disappear after this year.
Business organisations and trade unions were united in condemning the move.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said it was unhappy. "While robust consumer spending points to robust growth in the short term, there is increasing evidence that the weakness in the export sector will slow the pace of UK economic growth significantly during 1998," CBI chief economic adviser Kate Barker said in a statement.
"Strong sterling means serious problems for many companies today. We are concerned that this will exacerbate these difficulties in the months to come."
The British Chambers of Commerce described the rate rise as a "body blow" to exporters.

"This is the last thing Britain's exporters and their suppliers need at this time," BCC deputy director-general Ian Peters said. "If sterling continues to rise, fuelled by interest rate hikes, the result will be highly damaging to profits, investment and jobs and so the UK economy as a whole."
The Trades Union Congress (TUC) said the rate rise could put jobs at risk.
"The latest interest rate rise will put jobs at risk by keeping the pound high and slowing the economy next year," TUC deputy general secretary Brendan Barber said in a statement.
He said the "windfalls" from building society flotations were a one-off factor which did not pose a long-term threat to the government's 2.5 percent inflation target.
"Higher interest rates will do nothing to encourage industry to invest in skills and new capacity...the real barriers to continued expansion in 1998 and beyond," Barber added.
($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
